topic: Memory Hierarchy and Caching Strategies: Layered Structure
explanation: A memory hierarchy is a tiered structure of storage devices organized by decreasing speed, increasing capacity, and decreasing cost per bit. Faster, smaller levels (e.g., CPU registers and L1/L2 caches) serve as high-speed buffers for slower, larger levels (e.g., main memory and secondary storage). This layered design fundamentally exploits the principle of locality of reference—both temporal and spatial—to predict data needs. By ensuring frequently accessed data resides in the upper, faster tiers, the hierarchy minimizes the average memory access time (AMAT) and significantly enhances overall system performance.
